rules.rule: When explaining a research design, define it in both Korean and English and then explain the sample-time logic in one concrete example.
rules.reason: The professor repeatedly asked for the English labels and then pushed the class to explain what gets measured, when, and for whom.

rules.rule: Do not treat cross-sectional results as proof of age change; explicitly separate age difference from age change.
rules.reason: The lecture emphasized that comparing different age groups at one time point does not automatically show how the same people changed over time.

rules.rule: When interpreting an observed difference, check whether it is better explained by age effect, cohort effect, or period effect.
rules.reason: The professor treated this three-way distinction as the core reading lesson in developmental research methods.

rules.rule: Do not dismiss cross-sectional design as simply inferior; explain both its strengths and its limits.
rules.reason: The lecture explicitly defended cross-sectional studies on cost, speed, and the absence of repeated-measure learning effects.

rules.rule: When discussing longitudinal design, mention why it is valuable for aging research and also name attrition, survivor bias, repeated-measure learning effects, and cost or time burden.
rules.reason: The professor framed longitudinal research as powerful but methodologically demanding rather than automatically perfect.

rules.rule: For advanced designs, focus less on memorizing labels and more on why mixed or sequential designs are used to partially separate age, cohort, and period effects.
rules.reason: The professor said students do not need to recite every design name if they understand why researchers keep splitting designs this way.

rules.rule: Use the long-term case examples to explain method, not just to retell the story.
rules.reason: The Harvard longitudinal study and later Korean examples were used to show how research design creates certain kinds of evidence about aging.
